newsitem.title: FRANCE: Trichet not weakened by BoF changes - Boissonnat.
newsitem.headline: Trichet not weakened by BoF changes - Boissonnat.

text.p: Jean Boissonnat, leaving the Bank of France after three years on its monetary policy council (CPM), said on Monday that the appointment of two new members to the CPM would not weaken bank governor Jean-Claude Trichet.

The government on Friday appointed Pierre Guillen and Jean-Rene Bernard to the council, replacing Boissonnat and Bruno de Maulde, seen as staunch supporters of Trichet's policy of defending the stability of the franc against the mark.

Asked by Europe 1 radio whether the new appointments to the nine-member council would weaken Trichet, Boissonnat said: "weakened, I do not think so because...the two new arrivals are people who are aware of the responsibility they are taking on.

"I do not believe the appointment of the two people who have been chosen means that all of a sudden the monetary policy council has lost all its independence. It would be really exaggerating to say that. The two people who were chosen are completely respectable, they have experience. They are not young people. They are not revolutionaries, they are not agitators," he added.

Economists have said the appointment of Guillen and Bernard, who are seen as close to President Jacques Chirac, would increase the government's leverage over the Bank of France, which was made independent in 1994.
They may also swell the ranks of members of the council, in a minority until now, who have argued in favour of a slightly faster pace of interest rate cuts.
Boissonnat said there had always been a debate within the council, although this was about tactics rather than strategy.
"There was a lot of debate...we were lucky to have as a president Jean-Claude Trichet, who had only one vote like the rest of us and who is a man who loves to debate," he said.

"We discussed strategy -- stability, financing of the economy, preparations for Maastricht (European monetary union) -- on which we were very broadly in agreement, and then (we debated) tactics --- whether to go faster (in cutting rates) or to go cautiously," he said.
